title: The proud fall
hookLine: the one who is proud of power will fall (Sukhmani 12)

lines: AND ONE MORE NAME ON THE LIST.
THE ONE PROUD OF BEING GOOD.
cards: Guru Arjan makes a list in the first stanza of the twelfth ashtpadi, and it reads like a lineup of the people the world envies. The one with power. The one who is young and good-looking.
The one with money and land. You'd expect a hymn about pride to stop there. It doesn't.
Slipped into the same list, right beside the rich and the beautiful, is someone who seems to belong on the other team entirely: the person who is proud of being good.

teach.b: Yesterday's salok said the proud are worn away by their own pride.
Now the stanza shows what that pride looks like, one kind per line, each with a blunt picture of where it ends. Whoever carries the pride of ruling, the text says, sinks as low as a dog.
Whoever thinks, I am young and beautiful, ends up a worm in filth. The images are harsh on purpose; Guru Arjan isn't polite about something he thinks is dangerous.
Then the turn, before the stanza even reaches wealth: whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds wanders through birth after birth.
Only then comes wealth: whoever is proud of money and land, he calls a blind, ignorant fool. The good-deeds line is the one that stops a reader.
The Guru Granth Sahib praises good deeds, and Sikh life is full of them: serving in the langar, giving to people in need, standing up for the weak. So what's wrong with doing good? Nothing.
The warning is about the calling yourself. Good done and then worn like a medal becomes the same as the crown and the bank account: something to stand on, something to be seen with.

teach.h: AHANKAAR: THE VOICE THAT SAYS I.
teach.b: The salok's word for the proud was ahankaaree, from ahankaar, ego, the voice that says: I did this.
The pride is the same in all four, and so is the fall. Pride needs height, and height means a drop. The bigger the pedestal, the farther down the floor.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the stanzas of the twelfth ashtpadi, which name pride of power, beauty, wealth and good deeds, and Sikh teaching on seva prizes service done without show.

o: anger at someone who has wronged you
healthy confidence in your own abilities
ego, the inner voice that says I did this

games.q: the proud fall — tap the pairs.
p: sinks as low as a dog
I am a doer of good deeds

s: the twelfth ashtpadi warns only the rich and powerful
it also names the person proud of being good.
the stanza uses deliberately harsh pictures for pride
a dog, a worm in filth: Guru Arjan is blunt about danger.
the stanza says doing good deeds is a mistake
the warning is about calling yourself good, not about doing good.

games.q: you've volunteered every weekend for a year. someone asks how you spend your Saturdays. by the twelfth ashtpadi, where's the danger?
o: in wearing the good deed like a medal.
there's no danger in good deeds at all.
games.why: the stanza names whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds. the good is fine; the calling yourself is the pedestal.

practice: Sit quietly and let the mind run until it brings up something like, I handled that well, or I'm not like those people, or at least I'm the one who helps.
When it does, don't scold it; notice it the way you'd notice a car going by, name it softly, pride, and let it pass. Even catching one is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Ahankaar, pride, ego. Pride of power, of youth, of wealth, and even of good deeds: the voice that says I did this, and every pedestal has a drop.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ahankaar, pride, ego; the sense of making a me.

carryVoice: Your line: pride falls. Good done quietly needs no pedestal. Day four hundred eighty-three counts.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 12, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278)
